records.title: Show HN: Atticus – Hold-to-talk voice assistant for macOS that runs on Claude -p
records.author: SaarthRanka
records.storyText:
Hi HN! I'm Saarth. I'm in 9th grade, and I built Atticus.

Atticus is a fast and cheap Mac assistant that can do tasks for you. You hold down Control-Option-Space, speak or type your task, be it complex or a simple browser search, and Atticus will get on it.

The interesting part is that simple tasks, like opening apps, playing a Spotify playlist, or web queries, don't touch AI, and instead are processed locally and typically finish in under a second. For example, prompting Atticus to open apps takes around 0.08 seconds, sometimes even finishing before you finish your sentence, sort of like Jev.

Any tasks that are more complicated will be sent to Claude via claude -p, meaning you never need an API key and Atticus will run on your existing Claude Pro or Max plan. By using this approach, costs are also cut down immensely, with, on average, tasks costing a fraction of a cent.

To achieve Atticus' speed, it remembers shortcuts from each task it completes. When it does a task right for the first time, it saves its steps and replays them the next time without AI. For example, a workflow of creating a new meeting took about 30 seconds the first time around. Atticus then logs the exact steps to memory and takes 5-8 seconds on the next pass. To add to this, Atticus also learns about you as you use it more and from what's on your computer, including your name, your apps, and things you want it to remember, personalizing its answers to you.

To combat the safety concerns over giving an AI unrestricted access to your device, Atticus has toggleable restrictions, so before anything is deleted, sent, bought, or written to a file, the user is prompted before that action.

Some features I'm currently working on include a meeting copilot that capitalizes on Atticus' speed, allowing Atticus to listen in on meetings and answer questions in real time as they come in, personalized to the context of the meeting and what it knows about you.

To run Atticus, macOS 26 or higher is required for its voice transcription features. The voice transcription is also done locally by macOS.

Atticus is free, open source, and also very fresh, and I'm completely aware of its many rough edges, which is why I'd love to hear from everyone about what breaks and what you guys would like to see Atticus do!

records.title: Show HN: BraiNOTES, handwritten notes on your lecture PDFs in a browser tab
records.author: swimmingbrain
records.storyText:
In August, I posted here about TeXbrain, a LaTeX editor that runs completely in the browser, with no need for an account or server. (I didn't excpect it to get that much feedback, bug reports and help from here!)

This is the same idea for the other half of my studies, the handwritten notes. I take them on a convertible laptop, and I've had a hard time with apps for that, taking notes from a device to another, exporting as PDF, needing an account for many of them, etc. So I've been working on the version of it that I always wanted. Open a tab, the slides of the lecture or multiple PDFs open next to the page or even become the page, write on them with my pen, and nothing ever leaves my browser.

braiNOTES is a static website and has no backend. Strokes are perfect-freehand outlines which support pen pressure, the PDF files are rendered by pdf.js in a worker, and for storage it uses IndexedDB a moment after every change. No account, no analytics, and completely offline and local-first. You can export notebooks as .brainotes files, which in the background is a zip with one json per page + the PDFs and pictures you import. It keeps the original pages and puts the vectorized ink on top, this way the text stays selectable in the slides.

You can try it here: https://notes.swimmingbrain.dev GitHub Repo: https://github.com/swimmingbrain/brainotes (MIT)

In Study mode, the PDF opens on the side of the tab, you can read it simultaneously to the notes, snip a formula or diagrams directly into the notes with the snip tool, and then write around it. In Board mode, you have just a Whiteboard for tutoring or simply for more place for exercises, and can also highlight or draw things with the laser pointer tool while presenting.

The line of the ink appears the moment the pen moves, and a one euro filter calms shaky hands while you write + a light a refit when you lift the pen.

I also have a video editor and an animation tool which are still a work in progress, on the same GitHub profile. I'm also working on a MCP server for each tool, so you can use your MCP client to do further things with your notes, automatically edit videos on the video editor, etc. That feature will of course be off unless you turn it on and will only be able to talk to localhost.

I've used this tool for every lecture in the last few months and a few friends use it too. Bug reports, fixes, recommendations, feedback are all welcome!

records.title: Show HN: I Cut my Agent Tokens By 50%
records.author: iohotspot
records.storyText:
This started by watching the built-in tool calls in Claude code. We noticed that a LOT of the time was being spent searching for lines of code with regex. This approach makes sense when you are working in an unknown environment, but we all work inside of some codebase structure and tracking. This took us down the rabbit hole of codebase indexing and led to us building Indexio. Indexio was built to eliminate the time and tokens agents waste rediscovering a codebase. Regex calls return lots of data each time to the context window which causes bloat over time with items that don't really matter. Since codebase work container mostly static files indexing them and quickly getting to data for discovery is what we were trying to solve.

Indexio index's the codebase to its internal DB and then returns what is needed via MCP when asked. We ran into some fun issues when trying to force the session to use a tool call for lookups so there is some aggressive tool call logic which attempts to override built-in lookup tools. If something isn't in the index it will just fallback to regex lookups.

The whole system is a single binary written in Rust for performance. In our real world testing we are seeing about 50%-60% reduction in token usage compared to the built-in tools, and near instant lookup times compared to multiple seconds for each regex lookup. One place that indexio does come up shorter than then regex is when looking up symbols. We found that most of the agent's work was done looking at strings of words rather than symbols, but if you have a workflow that is heavy in this specific situation just know it may not fit.

We opened sourced everything and would love to hear feedback. Huge Shout out to CocoIndex who gave us the inspiration for this idea.

https://github.com/IOServicesLabs/indexio

records.title: Show HN: I built Airlock, to sandbox your AI agent and know what it's doing
records.author: simonmaddox
records.storyText:
I didn't like that Claude and codex effectively have the ability to do anything they want on my laptop and my local network - we've all read the horror stories of files accidentally being deleted - and while their permission classifier is getting better, it still requires a lot of trust. So I built Airlock for macOS which runs your agent in a virtual machine, and it will tell you exactly what it's run and what's changed before you bring anything back to your project. You can limit internet access to specific hosts, or block it altogether. It even works with Xcode projects (iOS and macOS developers rejoice). Technically you can run any command with Airlock - not just AI agents (`airlock run -- somecommand`).

It's free, requires no account, and has no tracking or analytics. I'm hoping Apple will approve it for Mac App Store distribution, but in the meantime you can download it directly from the website or using Homebrew.

records.title: Show HN: Lemma, an IDE for reading mathematics (macOS, open source)
records.author: fus3r
records.storyText:
I built Lemma while working through The Elements of Statistical Learning (using the Preview app). Kept running into references like "(3.41)" or "by Theorem 2.3" forcing me to scroll back through the entire book. And whenever a proof wasn’t detailed enough, I'd screenshot it, ask ChatGPT to explain, then go back to the PDF to add manual notes. Got pretty annoying.

That led me to Lemma: it reads a PDF once (locally), lets you jump around between equations, theorems, etc. without constantly scrolling. I gave it a VS Code look because yes, I'm addicted to VS Code (there are other themes for normal people).

A non-exhaustive list of things it can do (right now):

- References to theorems, equations, figures, citations and index entries are all clickable (you can peek at them without leaving the page)

- You can ask an agent or ChatGPT Web for explanations, longer proofs with one click, save the output in Lemma

- When the pdf says “it is easy to show” or “proof left to the reader”, you can write the missing steps in LaTeX, and Lemma checks it on random numerical inputs and gives counterexamples if it’s wrong.

You can also fold proofs to try them yourself first, and keep notes attached to specific passages (with exports to Markdown, Anki and Jupyter).

Built in Swift/SwiftUI using PDFKit. The analysis runs in a helper process at low priority. No account, no telemetry, and it's GPL. It’s for macOS 15+ only for now (unless a lot of people find it useful, then I’ll probably do it for other OSes). It still struggles with some PDFs (scanned ones, other languages, different numbering, etc.)

If you try it on whatever you're reading and encounter some problems, feel free to open an issue!

records.title: Show HN: A calendar of every Chinese holiday your supplier will cite as a delay
records.author: drk1rd
records.storyText:
If you've ever ordered anything from a factory in China, you've been given a delivery date of "after Chinese New Year." This is a site built around that.

What it does:

- Live status: is your supplier on holiday right now, based on China time and the official PRC holiday schedule. - Two windows per holiday: the official days off from the State Council, and the "factory reality" window, when production actually stops. For Chinese New Year 2027 (Feb 6), that's ~8–9 official days off vs. roughly Jan 23 to mid-March of real disruption. - A rough ETA calculator: it walks your quoted lead time day by day through every closure and slowdown, then adds QC and transit time. Example: an order on Dec 15 with a quoted 30 days to Europe lands around May 7, not late February. - A subscribable .ics feed with alerts before the big shutdowns. - A plain table of all 2026–2027 holidays: /holidays - A CNY 2027 checklist and timeline for importers: /cny

Notes:

- The 2026 dates follow the official State Council schedule. The 2027 festival dates are fixed by the lunar calendar, but the exact days off and weekend make-up workdays are usually published in Nov–Dec, so those are marked TBA. The calendar feed will update when they're out. - The "factory reality" windows are heuristics from common industry patterns, not data from any one factory. Corrections from people who actually deal with this are very welcome. - It's fully static: no backend, no accounts, no analytics. Bingo cards and checklists live in localStorage. - Some of it is satire (the supplier phrasebook, the "unofficial festivals"). The jokes are aimed at buyers who order in December and act surprised in February, not at the holidays, which are real and well deserved.

records.title: Show HN: I added optional chaining to CPython
records.author: grandimam
records.storyText:
I forked CPython to experiment with adding optional chaining (?.) directly to the language.

For example: name = response?.customer?.name.lower()

If response or customer is None, the expression short-circuits and evaluates to None. This isn't a library or a transpiler change, but a direct CPython modification.

A bit about the build: I used AI extensively for this experiment. Part of my motivation was to see how far I can get the modification in an unfamiliar codebase like CPython.

A couple of hours in I had a working prototype. I would appreciate feedback from people familiar with CPython internals about the implementation.

Source: https://github.com/grandimam/cpython

records.title: Show HN: Vocafy – Listen to Vocaloid songs by producer, from the original videos
records.author: piro0919
records.storyText:
I built Vocafy, a music player web app for Vocaloid songs. You pick songs by producer, singer (voicebank), or year, and it plays the original videos from YouTube and Niconico.

Around 2010-2012, at the peak of the Vocaloid boom, I made music videos for a Vocaloid producer. I skipped university for days to edit videos, and it was honestly the most fulfilling time of my life. Lately Vocaloid songs seem to be showing up on YouTube again, so I thought now was the time to give something back. I built it together with Claude Code.

In my opinion, Vocaloid is mainly about the songs, not the videos. But there aren't many services focused on the songs. YouTube and Niconico are video services. YouTube Music mixes covers and unauthorized reuploads in with the originals, and its search isn't great, so it's hard to reach the song you want among the huge number of Vocaloid songs.

Features:

- Browse by voicebank, year, or producer

- Favorite songs and producers (sign in with Google to sync across devices)

- Continuous play, shuffle, and radio

- A picture-in-picture-like mini player

- Sleep timer

- Both YouTube and Niconico

- Add to home screen to use it as an app (Android, iOS, PC)

- Theme colors based on Vocaloid characters

Because of technical limits, background playback and continuous Niconico playback on iOS Safari are hard to support.

As of October 2026 there are about 30,000 songs, 800 producers, and 700 singers, and I add more every week. It's completely free. If a song you're looking for is missing, let me know.

English isn't my first language, so I wrote this in Japanese and used AI to translate it.

records.title: Show HN: PanamaKVM – direct-booting Linux from Java 25 via FFM/KVM
records.author: rusanoph
records.storyText:
Hi HN, author here.

Why I built it: I wanted to test whether the FFM API (java.lang.foreign) is mature enough to talk directly to a real kernel API like KVM, without JNI or native glue code.

What it does today: PanamaKVM is a minimal VMM written in Java 25. It talks to /dev/kvm through FFM downcalls, direct-boots an x86-64 Linux kernel and gives you an interactive serial console.

The interesting technical part: there is no JNI, no C shim and no project-owned native library. The VMM/control plane is entirely Java; the only native code involved is libc and the KVM ioctl.

The ioctl/strace story: my very first call, KVM_GET_API_VERSION, returned EINVAL even though /dev/kvm, permissions and modules were all fine. The Java debugger didn't help much, but strace did: the syscall reached the kernel with an unexpected third argument. libc's ioctl is variadic and passes its third argument through to the syscall, while my FunctionDescriptor only declared fd and request, so that slot was undefined. The KVM handler returns -EINVAL for a nonzero arg. The fix was declaring a third argument and passing 0L explicitly. A FunctionDescriptor is effectively an executable claim about the ABI, and the JVM can't check it against the KVM docs for you.

What is verified: a pinned Alpine 3.24.2 x86-64 kernel boots into a BusyBox initramfs userspace and gives an interactive shell. That is the only guest I have tested; I make no claims about broader compatibility.

What is deliberately missing: virtio, networking, persistent storage, SMP (single vCPU only). It also has no production-grade hardening and is not designed to run hostile guests.

Feedback I would like:

- Review of the FFM usage: FunctionDescriptors, struct layouts, arena/lifetime management and the ioctl wrapper design.

- Whether there are useful applications beyond education/experimentation that I haven't considered

Happy to answer questions.

records.title: Show HN: search for AI agents that flags pages later news replaced
records.author: Ayobamiu
records.storyText:
I built this at a Berkeley hackathon with Simon Kley. It’s a search layer for AI agents. Each result comes back with a usefulness score and a price before the agent reads it, plus a flag when a later story has replaced the page.

What pushed us toward freshness: when an agent started from an outdated news alert, it wrote stale sales outreach in 4 of 7 cases, even though the newer story was in the pages it had read. Our check caught 4 of 4 replaced pages with no false alarms on 5 controls. On a sales research task (n=15), the agent read 3.1 pages instead of 10.

Caveats: these are small samples, prices are simulated, and our version used more tokens than the baseline (19.5k vs 14.1k). The demo runs locally for now.

I’d especially like to hear from people running research agents in production. How do you deal with outdated pages today?

records.title: Show HN: An open source AI leaderboard of the best models your machine can run
records.author: jakemanger
records.storyText:
Hi everyone, I made whatmodel. It's a simple site that can be visited in the browser or used from the terminal via a:

curl whatmodel.sh

To use it,

1. Enter your RAM and GPU

2. See what models you can run locally with its rank and the command to run it

3. Compare them with API models on the same score

Building it made me realise a 32GB Mac can now run a model that scores on par with GPT-5, completely locally and for free (e.g. Qwen 3.8 27B at 4-bit).

Each model gets one score fitted across 18,731 published benchmark results, and every result links to its source.

The method is at https://whatmodel.sh/method and the data, scoring code and bench script are open source: https://github.com/jakemanger/whatmodel

If you'd like to contribute, there's a bench script to collect real-world tok/s and you can also submit any new models and benchmark scores along with their source on github.

records.title: Show HN: Tracon (air traffic control for subagents)
records.author: allocate
records.storyText:
My Claude Code workflow usually involves... a lot of subagents. I make one Opus model coordinate work as my tech lead, it dispatches subagents using models appropriate for the task into their own git worktrees, and then I try to multitask and do something else while they run.

I'd been finding lately (particularly with Opus 5.5) that there was a ton of drift and instances of subagents not doing anything and it was evading the attention of the TL despite the instructions I gave it to have them report in at a regular cadence.

Running tracon in a split terminal is my new personal workflow. It gives me early indicators when things start going off the rails (ex. blocked on a prompt, idle, looping on a failing command, simultaneous edits to files other subagents are editing, drifting off the brief, etc.) and I can interrogate the subagent's workflow and by pressing n the main agent gets a note to make a call on how and if to correct it.

Read-only and runs on your machine: it tails transcripts in ~/.claude/projects/ and checks each worktree with ps, lsof, and git -- only thing that leaves your machine is what the Haiku judge reads for classification (or optionally you can turn that off with --no-judge).

I've found it super useful for the game I'm building and figured others in the community might also find it useful.

If you just want to give it a spin without committing:

  uvx tracon --demo
macOS and Linux, Python 3.12+, MIT. (Not affiliated with Anthropic.)

records.title: Show HN: Tilefinch – a from-scratch* web browser for the PSP (333Mhz, 64MB RAM)
records.author: stjanovitz
records.storyText:
I picked up my PSP for the first time in about a decade and wanted to find out three things: how far the hardware could be pushed, how much of the modern web fits on it, and what today’s coding agents can do. A web browser tests all three.

Tilefinch runs entirely on a PSP-3000: networking, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, layout and rendering, over Wi-Fi, with no proxy or companion computer. The style, layout, paint, media and UI layers are new C code and a patched QuickJS runs the JavaScript.

Each page gets a single 32 MB budget covering DOM, JavaScript, CSS, images, layout and tiles.

A few things that work: logged-out ChatGPT rendering a response; YouTube and HTML video through the PSP’s hardware decoder, at up to 360p; Canvas 2D and WebGL 1 on the PSP’s graphics chip (the repo includes a new 3D tank game as a demo). There's also modern browser features like Reader mode, dark mode, an ad blocker, language packs and in-app updates.

However, some sites are too large (in which the browser offers a "Basic" mode) and most are slow to render.

records.title: Show HN: How good is your Rust? Free quiz, every code answer checked by rustc
records.author: grajo
records.storyText:
I run rustcoach, an AI-guided Rust course. This is the free, no-signup part of it: a 30-question test across core Rust, async/Tokio, macros, concurrency/atomics and the type system, plus a 20-question test for each of those areas if you want to dig depper (also free, no registration). At the end you get a level, a per-area breakdown and a suggestion of what to learn next.

I don't know any other site which allows you to test your Rust knowledge in a comprehensive way like mine but would be great to hear about others and/or suggestions to this one.

You can take it multiple times and will get a different set of questions either in general rust category or if you are brave enough and know deeper any other popular areas of Rust like macros, async with Tokio etc you can try your luck there. There is over 600 questions in the pool.

The general test with 30 questions should take more or less around 10 mintues but of course every one reads code at different speed so the time needed to complete the test may vary - and reading the questions really carefully is very important in this case :)

Hope you like it, if so share it, comment and let's become better Rust programmers. I have a feeling that with AI doing all the work now, this will be rather diminishing skill in the IT world.

The compiler can confirm that a snippet does what the answer says.

records.title: Show HN: Atlas Runa – E2E AI-enhanced language learning
records.author: eamost
records.storyText:
Hi HN! We've been working hard on Atlas Runa and it's time to share it! We built it to target three key complementary aspects of learning a language: 1. Comprehensible input - Atlas Runa learns your lexicon and then tracks it, which lets us find comprehensible input for you. This works well already. You can start reading real texts and get reading volume much earlier than you would ever be able to with textbooks! 2. The attention effect - we track your mistakes and what you forget and make sure to bring it back so you can drill it 3. Good content - we work really hard authoring quality non-slop content at graded levels so learning stays fun. Intrinsic motivation is the best kind of motivation!

Please give it a try and let us know what you think!
